introduction: Is God within the world or beyond it? These readings refuse to choose in the way the question expects. They say that God is nearer than nearness, with a person wherever he is, and that every particle carries a sign of Him; and they say as firmly that His essence is beyond every mind, does not descend into creation, does not incarnate, and is not divided among His creatures. The sun and the mirror carry much of the argument: the light is truly in the mirror, and the sun has not come down. Isaiah, the Psalms, the Qur’an, the Isha Upanishad and Augustine hold near and far together in the same way. The quotations set against the readings come from those who placed God in the world or in the self: Spinoza, the Stoics, the Chandogya Upanishad, Emerson and Whitman, with the Gospel of John and Colossians on the Word made flesh. Wordsworth, Hopkins and the Gita stand between, and ask where a sign ends and a presence begins.
questions: The readings say that God is manifest in all things and yet sanctified above all things. What is the difference between finding a sign of God in something and finding God in it?
Spinoza, the Stoics and the Chandogya Upanishad each place the divine within the world or the self. What do the readings grant to that view, and where do they stop?
John’s Gospel says the Word was made flesh; the readings say the Essence does not incarnate, and use the picture of the sun in a mirror. What does the mirror keep that both sides want to say?
Xenophanes said that oxen would draw their gods as oxen. How would you know if the God you pray to is one of your own contriving?
If the essence of God cannot be known, what is a person turning toward in prayer?
Isaiah’s high and lofty One dwells with the contrite. When has God seemed nearest to you, and what had that to do with greatness or with lowliness?

outside.why: Tennyson wrote of God that closer is He than breathing, and nearer than hands and feet.
Shelley asked the wind to make him its lyre and to drive his dead thoughts over the universe like withered leaves.
The psalmist finds that there is nowhere to flee from that presence, not in heaven nor in the uttermost parts of the sea.
The Qur’an says that God is nearer to a person than his jugular vein.
The psalm calls on sun, moon and stars of light to praise their maker.
The Isha Upanishad says of the highest reality that it stirs and stirs not, and is far and likewise near.
Spinoza held that whatever is, is in God, and nothing can be or be conceived without God. Where does manifest in all yet sanctified above all part company with him?
These are the words of the Qur’an that the reading repeats: He is with you wheresoever ye may be.
Jeremiah hears God ask: am I a God at hand and not a God afar off? Do not I fill heaven and earth?
Wordsworth felt a presence whose dwelling is the light of setting suns, that rolls through all things. Is a sign of God in every particle the same as a spirit dwelling in every particle?
Moses asked to see God's glory and was told that no one can see His face and live; he saw only what passed by.
Isaiah asks: to whom then will ye liken God, or what likeness will ye compare unto Him?
The psalm asks who is like the Lord, who dwells on high and humbles Himself to behold the things in heaven and earth.
Solomon, dedicating the temple he had built, admitted that the heaven of heavens cannot contain God.
Job says that all we know are parts of His ways, and how little a portion is heard of Him.
Isaiah's high and lofty One who inhabits eternity says that He dwells also with the contrite and humble. How can the most exalted be the nearest?
One of Job's friends asks whether anyone can by searching find out God.
The Qur’an says that vision comprehends Him not, but He comprehends all vision.
The Tao Te Ching opens by saying that the way that can be trodden is not the enduring way, nor the name that can be named the enduring name.

Whitman tells mankind not to be curious about God, since he sees God in every object and every hour and understands Him not in the least. Is a closed door a reason to stop asking, or a reason to ask differently?
Jesus gave the Christian answer to the same question: no one comes to the Father but by him.
Kabir has God say: where dost thou seek Me? I am beside thee, neither in temple nor in mosque. Why would turning to the God who is everywhere not be enough?
John's Gospel says that no one has seen God at any time; the Son has declared Him.
The Letter to the Hebrews calls the Son the brightness of God's glory and the express image of His person.
Isaiah says it directly to God in the middle of a prophecy: verily Thou art a God that hidest Thyself.
Jesus tells Philip that whoever has seen him has seen the Father.
This is the saying the picture of the mirror explains: I and my Father are one.
Paul calls Christ the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature.
The letter to the Colossians says that in Christ dwells all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. Does the picture of the sun in a mirror say less than this, or say it more carefully?
Paul says that the knowledge of God's glory is given in the face of Jesus Christ.
This is the verse the Bedouin asked about: whithersoever ye turn, there is the face of God.
The Qur’an calls God the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward.
Genesis begins before there was anything: the earth without form, and the Spirit of God moving on the face of the waters.
Plotinus says that the One, seeking nothing and lacking nothing, has overflowed, and its exuberance has produced the new.
Paul told the Athenians that in God we live and move and have our being.
The Nicene Creed says that the Son is Light of Light, of one substance with the Father. Is the sun and its rays the creed's own picture, or a different account of the three?
Augustine, searching for words at the start of his Confessions, addresses God as most hidden and most near.
The Qur’an's shortest statement of unity ends: there is none comparable unto Him.
Israel's daily confession is: hear, O Israel, the Lord our God is one Lord.
The psalm says that clouds and darkness are round about Him, and righteousness the habitation of His throne.
John's Gospel says that the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld his glory. How do the readings understand that verse, if God in no wise manifests His inmost Essence?
Paul exclaims at the depth of God's wisdom: how unsearchable are His judgments, and His ways past finding out.
Paul says that the invisible things of God are clearly seen from the creation, being understood by the things that are made.
The psalm says that the heavens declare the glory of God and the firmament shows His handiwork.
The Qur’an says that in the creation of the heavens and the earth there are signs for people who have sense.

Darwin looked at an entangled bank of plants, birds, insects and worms and saw forms produced by laws acting around us. Does an account of how the forms arose remove the need for a cause of their being?
Pascal said that if there is a God He is infinitely incomprehensible, having neither parts nor limits.
Kant concluded that he had to deny knowledge of such things in order to make room for faith.
Xenophanes remarked that if oxen and horses had hands they would draw their gods as oxen and horses.
The commandment forbids making any likeness of anything in heaven or earth to bow down to it.
Isaiah hears God say: my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways.
The Preacher advises: God is in heaven and thou upon earth, therefore let thy words be few.
Maimonides writes that God is one with a unity unlike any other unity in existence.
Paul told the Athenians that the God who made the world does not dwell in temples made with hands.
The letter to the Ephesians speaks of one God who is above all, and through all, and in you all.

Pope pictured one soul that warms in the sun, refreshes in the breeze, glows in the stars and blossoms in the trees. What is the difference between a God who contains all and a God who is the soul of all?
The Qur’an says that nothing is like Him, and He is the Hearer, the Seer.
Moses reminded Israel that they saw no manner of similitude on the day God spoke at Horeb.
Augustine looked for an image of the Trinity in love itself: one who loves, that which is loved, and love. What do the two explanations have in common, and what does each protect?
The Qur’an says that the Messiah, son of Mary, was no other than a messenger.
Emerson said that Jesus saw that God incarnates Himself in man, and that each of us may say, I am divine. What is lost, on the reading's account, when the vessel is taken for what it holds?
Dante says that the glory of Him who moves everything penetrates the universe and shines in one part more and in another less.
Xenophanes spoke of one god, greatest among gods and men, unlike mortals in form or in thought.

The Chandogya Upanishad teaches that the subtle essence of all that exists is the Self, and thou art it. How does that teaching differ from the view this reading attributes to the Sufis, and how does the reading answer both?
Krishna says in the Gita that all things hang on him as a row of pearls upon its string. Is the string in the pearls, or are the pearls on the string?
The first letter of John says that no one has seen God, and that if we love one another God dwells in us.
Hopkins wrote that the world is charged with the grandeur of God, which will flame out like shining from shook foil. How can the world be charged with what never descends into it?
Whitman declared himself divine inside and out, and holy whatever he touched. What would the reading say he had mistaken?
Plotinus compares what proceeds from the One to the light around the sun, generated ceaselessly while the source remains unaltered.
Plato says that the sun gives things their visibility and their growth, though it is not itself growth.
Marcus Aurelius asks us to regard the universe as one living being with one substance and one soul. What did the Stoics see truly, and what does the reading say they missed?
Seneca wrote that God is near you, with you, within you, and that a holy spirit dwells in us. Is the divine spark a figure of speech the readings can accept, or the doctrine they reject?
Julian of Norwich saw all that is made as a thing the size of a hazel-nut, lasting only because God loves it.
The Throne Verse says that His throne includes the heavens and the earth, and He is never weary of preserving them.
Elizabeth Barrett Browning wrote that earth is crammed with heaven and every common bush afire with God.
Whitman found letters from God dropped in the street, every one signed with God's name.
The psalm marvels that man is made a little lower than the angels and given dominion over the works of God's hands.
Augustine says that God has made us for Himself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in Him.
The letter to the Ephesians prays that its readers may know the love that passes knowledge.
Job asks where wisdom shall be found, since the depth says, It is not in me.
Milton addresses God as light who dwelt from eternity in unapproached light.
Jesus thanked the Father that these things are hidden from the wise and prudent and revealed to babes.
The psalm says that the Lord is nigh to those of a broken heart.
Paul says that we do not know what to pray for as we ought, and that the Spirit intercedes with groanings that cannot be uttered.
Dante, at the end of his vision, can only address a light that alone knows itself.
The Qur’an says that the seven heavens and the earth and all within them hymn His praise, though you do not understand their praise.
The psalm calls its hearers to worship and bow down and kneel before the Lord their maker.
When a crowd took Paul and Barnabas for gods come down, they tore their clothes and said they were men of like nature.
Spinoza taught that whoever loves God cannot endeavour that God should love him in return. What is at stake in saying that God has a mind, a will and a purpose?
Aristotle's God is thought thinking itself, since it could think of nothing less excellent. Is a God who is conscious of His creation greater or less than that?
Job says: I go forward, but He is not there, and backward, but I cannot perceive Him.
The psalm says that the Lord is nigh unto all who call upon Him in truth. How does a worshipper pray to a God who is beyond every attribute?
The first letter to Timothy says that there is one God and one mediator between God and men.
The psalm says of idols that they have eyes and see not, and that those who make them are like them.
Tennyson called our systems of thought broken lights of God, who is more than they.
Augustine asked the earth, the sea and the heavens, and each answered: I am not He, but He made us.
The Light Verse of the Qur’an calls God the light of the heavens and the earth, light upon light.
The Chandogya Upanishad says that in the beginning there was only that which is, one only, without a second.
Pascal held that it is the heart which experiences God, and not the reason.
Kant found two things that fill the mind with awe: the starry heavens above and the moral law within.

exodus-no-man-see-me-and-live.text: And he said, Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live. And the Lord said, Behold, there is a place by me, and thou shalt stand upon a rock: And it shall come to pass, while my glory passeth by, that I will put thee in a clift of the rock, and will cover thee with my hand while I pass by: And I will take away mine hand, and thou shalt see my back parts: but my face shall not be seen

romans-invisible-things-clearly-seen.text: For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse

colossians-fulness-of-the-godhead.text: For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily

psalm-nigh-unto-all-that-call.text: The Lord is nigh unto all them that call upon him, to all that call upon him in truth

psalm-who-is-like-unto-the-lord.text: Who is like unto the Lord our God, who dwelleth on high, Who humbleth himself to behold the things that are in heaven, and in the earth

quran-with-you-wheresoever.text: and He is with you wheresoever ye may be. And Allah is Seer of what ye do

isha-far-and-near.text: It stirs and it stirs not; it is far, and likewise near
